cards.title: THE PATIO OR DECK
cards.tagline: SIX ZONES. THE SURFACE AND THE RAIL COME FIRST.
cards.objective: A patio lives outdoors, on a clock the indoor rooms never feel. This card is the map and the order.
zones_in_order: PDZ-002 Grill and Outdoor Cooking Zone
PDZ-004 Garden and Plant Care Zone
PDZ-006 Surface, Rail, and Safety Zone
cards.start_here: PDZ-006 Surface, Rail, and Safety Zone. Do the Surface, Rail, and Safety Zone first, on a dry morning, before you touch a single cushion. If the boards and the railing are not sound, everything you arrange on top of them is decoration.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the six ZONE cards face up. Start with the Surface, Rail, and Safety Zone on a dry morning, before you touch a single cushion.
2. Lay out that zone's three FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true on your patio. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 2. Cleaning out here is how you inspect: you will never spot a popped fastener, a soft board end, or a spider web in a burner tube while sitting in a chair.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do PDA-013 The Full Patio Hazard Walk before any rebuild. It takes thirty minutes and covers the rail and boards, the grease tray and tank, the chemical box latch, and the deck box lid stay in one pass.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Sun-aged plastic and resin chairs fail suddenly at the leg joint, and they fail under the person least able to catch themselves.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: A folded lounger or a stacked chair left across the route between the door and the steps is the thing people trip on carrying a tray in the dark.

the_call.title: The speckled cushion
the_call.text: You have a cushion with grey and black speckling along the piping. It got rained on, it went into the box damp, and every spring you tell yourself you will scrub it properly. Give it exactly one honest attempt: wash it with a fabric cleaner meant for outdoor material, dry it fully in sun, and put it back. If the speckling returns within the same season, the growth is inside the foam core and no surface cleaning reaches it. That cushion is finished. Replace it or go without, and either is better than a seat nobody chooses. The pattern to break is buying replacement cushions before you have fixed the reason the last set died, which was that they had nowhere dry to go in a hurry.

cards.title: GRILL AND OUTDOOR COOKING ZONE
cards.tagline: FOUR TOOLS ON THE HOOKS. THE TANK LEVEL MARKED ON THE COLLAR.
cards.objective: Cook over fire without leaving the grill to find a tool or wondering if there is gas.
callouts: Grates scraped bare of built-up residue
An empty grease tray sitting back in its rails
Exactly four tools hanging on the grill's own hooks, nothing extra
A propane tank standing upright with its fuel level marked on the collar
A clear arm's length of open air between the grill body and the siding
No fifth tool anywhere near the hooks
cards.done_looks_like: Grates scraped bare, grease tray emptied and back in its rails, four tools on the grill's own hooks and no fifth anywhere, the propane tank upright with its level written on the collar, and a clear arm's length between the grill body and the siding, railing, and umbrella canopy.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Accumulated grease in the tray and drip pan is what turns a normal flare-up into a fire, and a grill within reach of siding, decking rail, or a canopy gives that fire somewhere to go.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Bristles shed from a worn wire brush stick to the grates and then to food, and a swallowed bristle is a genuine emergency.

the_call.title: The tank you are not sure about
the_call.text: You have two propane tanks and no idea which has gas in it, so you keep buying a third and the collection grows against the wall. Settle it with a bathroom scale. The tare weight is stamped on the collar as TW and a number; weigh the tank, subtract that number, and what remains is propane. If what is left would not carry you through one long cook with guests, that is a refill errand, not a spare. Write the answer on the collar in marker, and write it again the day a tank comes back from the exchange. While you are reading the collar, find the date stamp: tanks have a requalification life and the exchange counter will simply refuse an old one, which is worth knowing now rather than on a Saturday with people arriving. Two tanks is the right number. Anything beyond two is a storage problem pretending to be preparedness.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: An umbrella left open on an undersized base lifts in a gust and comes down pole first, usually across the table where people were sitting.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: Indoor extension leads run out to string lights or a speaker sit in rain and puddles on the boards, which is the one electrical shortcut outdoors that genuinely kills.

the_call.title: Its own set, or nothing
the_call.text: Decide once whether this table gets dishware of its own, because the half-answer is what keeps it covered. Count the meals you genuinely ate out here last season. If it was more than a handful, buy one stackable set, plates, tumblers, and flatware for the number of seats, and keep it in a lidded tote in the deck box so eating outdoors costs one trip. If it was two or three meals all year, admit that, and carry the indoor plates out on those few occasions. What you must stop is the middle option: storing four faded plates, a mismatched tumbler, and a serving bowl outdoors for a set you will never complete. That orphaned half-set is precisely why the table always has something standing on it, and why it never looks ready to sit down at.

cards.title: GARDEN AND PLANT CARE ZONE
cards.tagline: EMPTY SAUCERS. THE CHEMICALS LATCHED UP HIGH.
cards.objective: Keep the containers alive and keep everything that feeds them off the ground and out of reach.

cards.done_looks_like: Every saucer empty, pots nested by size along the wall with drain holes clear, one tool caddy holding trowel, pruners, and gloves, and a latched chemical box above the tools with no more in it than you can name from the doorway.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Slug pellets and fertilizer granules look like food to a dog, and a concentrate decanted into a drink bottle is the classic route to a poisoning in a house with children.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A large glazed pot full of wet soil is far heavier than it looks and it lands on feet; slide it on a wheeled saucer instead of lifting it.

the_call.title: The half bottles
the_call.text: There is a shelf of part-used concentrates: a weed killer bought for one path, a rooting hormone, a bug spray whose label has washed to nothing. You avoid this shelf because there is no easy way to get rid of them, and pouring them down a drain is not one. Two rules settle it. First, if you cannot read the label, that container is finished, no exceptions, because an unlabelled garden chemical cannot be used safely by you or by anyone who finds it later; it goes to the household hazardous waste collection. Second, if you can read it, ask whether you have used it in the last two growing seasons. If not, it goes the same way. What survives is a short row you can name from the doorway. From this point on, buy the smallest container the shop sells rather than the best value size, because the value size is what created this shelf.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: An unsupported deck box lid falls at hand height and catches fingers on the hinge side, which is where children reach when they help.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Mice nest in stored cushions and fabric, and shaking out contaminated bedding indoors sends droppings and dust into the air you breathe.

the_call.title: What the box is actually for
the_call.text: You bought the deck box for cushions, and now it holds everything on this patio that has nowhere else to be. So the cushions ride on a layer of pool toys and dead covers, they never go all the way down, and the lid stands half open in the rain. Decide the box's single job and hold it against pressure: it stores cushions, because cushions are the only thing out here that must be under a lid within a minute of the first drop. Everything else that has crept in gets a real home in the garage or leaves the property this weekend. Carrying it all out will look like waste while you are doing it. It is not. A box that cannot close protects nothing inside it, so the arrangement you have now is already costing you the cushions, one damp night at a time.

cards.title: SURFACE, RAIL, AND SAFETY ZONE
cards.tagline: PUSH THE RAIL HARD. IF IT MOVES, NOBODY STANDS ON IT TONIGHT.
cards.objective: The structure you stand on and lean against, kept sound and kept clear.
callouts: Nothing on the deck surface that is not furniture
Daylight visible through clear gaps between the boards
No green film on the shaded stair treads
A rail post standing immovable under a hard push
A dated tag hanging just inside the back door
Stair treads that rise the same height as the ones above and below
cards.done_looks_like: Nothing on the deck that is not furniture, daylight visible through the gaps between boards, no green film on the shaded treads, and every rail post immovable when you push it hard.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: A railing post that moves when you push it will not hold an adult who stumbles into it, and the drop off the side of a deck is onto whatever is stored below.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: Algae film on the shaded boards and the stair treads turns to grease after rain, and the treads are where a slip costs the most.

the_call.title: The board that gives
the_call.text: There is a board you step over without thinking, or one that flexes slightly under your weight, and you have quietly filed it as fine. Test it properly instead. Push a screwdriver into the board where it crosses a joist, and again into the board end nearest the house. If the tip sinks in with light pressure, that board is finished and replacing one board is a morning's work. The harder judgment is what a soft board is telling you. If two boards side by side are soft, or if the softness is at the ledger where the deck meets the wall of the house, then the framing underneath has the problem and the surface is only the symptom. The rule that settles it: soft in one spot on top, replace the board yourself; soft in two adjacent places or soft at the wall, stop putting people on it and get someone underneath it with a torch before the next time you have guests standing out here together.

cards.title: A CHAIR WITH A WOBBLE, A CRACKED ARM, OR A FLEXING SEAT IS STILL IN THE CIRCLE
cards.tagline: WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. THEN WHY.
cards.objective: A resin or plastic chair with a wobble, a cracked arm, or a seat pan that flexes when you press it hard is still standing in the evening seating circle instead of at the curb.

branches.answer: A chair failing under someone is a real fall risk, and that outranks how many of the other chairs still look fine standing there
There is no agreed point where a chair officially fails the standard, so it stays in rotation until it actually gives out under someone
It has creaked in that same spot for months, long enough that the sound stopped registering as a warning

steps: Carry the cushions into the deck box and fasten the latch, and scrape the grill's hot grates before you close the lid.
